# Bhaddāli Sutta (MN 65 (PTS MN i 437))
**ID:** MN 65 (PTS MN i 437)

**Title (Pali):** Bhaddāli Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Bhaddāli

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Bhaddāli Sutta* (MN 65) is set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthī [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. In the sutta, the Buddha instructs the monastics to eat in a single session (avoiding eating after midday), explaining that doing so ensures freedom from illness and brings lightness, physical strength, and comfort [SuttaCentral; French and Nathan 2014; Anālayo 2017; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The monk Bhaddāli openly refuses to comply, objecting that he cannot maintain his strength on a single meal [French and Nathan 2014; Anālayo 2017]. The Buddha reprimands Bhaddāli for his recalcitrance and employs rhetorical comparisons, such as asking whether a disciplined disciple would refuse a hypothetical request to serve as a bridge across mud for the Buddha [French and Nathan 2014; Flores 2008]. After persistent remorse, Bhaddāli confesses his transgression and receives the Buddha's pardon and counsel [Humphreys 1956; SuttaCentral]. The discourse also addresses monastic jurisprudence, clarifying that training rules were not laid down in the Sangha's earliest days; rather, rules are instituted only after moral corruptions arise as the community expands and gains fame [Sarao and Long 2017; Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010]. The sutta concludes with an exposition on spiritual maturation using the simile of training a thoroughbred colt (*assājānīya*) [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995].
Full parallels to the discourse survive in Chinese translation in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 194) and *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 49.7), alongside a Sanskrit fragment preserved in the Turfan findings (SHT sutta15) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus aligns these sections automatically with the *Madhyama-āgama* (ZH_T01_0026) and *Ekottarika-āgama* (ZH_T02_0125), and identifies cross-tradition alignments in Vinaya literature including the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Prātimokṣasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse with Khandhaka rules in the Vinaya (notably the *Campeyyakkhandhaka*, Kd 9) and shared doctrinal sequences found in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) and several numerical books of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (AN 3, AN 4, AN 5) [DharmaNexus].
